title: Book 3, Chapter 10 — Fifth Year of the War—Trial and Execution of the Plataeans— Corcyraean Revolution
paragraphs: During the same summer, after the reduction of Lesbos, the Athenians under Nicias, son of Niceratus, made an expedition against the island of Minoa, which lies off Megara and was used as a fortified post by the Megarians, who had built a tower on it. Nicias wanted to enable the Athenians to keep up their blockade from this nearer station instead of from Budorum and Salamis, to stop the Peloponnesian galleys and privateers from sailing out unobserved from the island, as they had been in the habit of doing, and at the same time to prevent anything from coming into Megara. Accordingly, after taking two towers projecting on the side of Nisaea by means of engines from the sea, and clearing the entrance into the channel between the island and the shore, he next set about cutting off all communication by building a wall on the mainland at the point where a bridge across a marsh enabled reinforcements to be thrown into the island, which was not far from the continent. A few days were enough to accomplish this. He afterwards raised some works on the island as well, and leaving a garrison there, departed with his forces.

About the same time in this summer, the Plataeans, now without provisions and unable to hold out under the siege, surrendered to the Peloponnesians in the following way. An assault had been made on the wall, which the Plataeans were unable to repel. The Lacedaemonian commander, seeing their weakness, did not want to take the place by storm. His instructions from Lacedaemon had been framed so that, if at some future date peace should be made with Athens and they should agree each to restore the places taken in the war, Plataea might be considered to have come over voluntarily and not be included in the list. He accordingly sent a herald to ask if they were willing to surrender the town to the Lacedaemonians voluntarily and accept them as their judges, with the understanding that the guilty would be punished, but no one without due process. The Plataeans were now in the last stage of weakness, and as soon as the herald had delivered his message, they surrendered the town. The Peloponnesians fed them for some days until the judges from Lacedaemon, who were five in number, arrived. On their arrival no charge was put forward; they simply called up the Plataeans and asked whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in the war then in progress. The Plataeans asked leave to speak at greater length, and deputed two of their number to represent them: Astymachus, son of Asopolaus, and Lacon, son of Aeimnestus, proxenus of the Lacedaemonians, who came forward and spoke as follows:

“Lacedaemonians, when we surrendered our city we trusted you, and we expected a trial more in keeping with the forms of law than the present one, which we never imagined being subjected to. The judges in whose hands we agreed to place ourselves were yourselves, and you alone — from whom we thought we were most likely to obtain justice — and not other people, as is now the case. As things stand, we are afraid that we have been doubly deceived. We have good reason to suspect not only that the issue to be tried is the most terrible of all, but that you will not prove impartial — judging by the fact that no charge was put first for us to answer, but we had to ask leave to speak ourselves, and that the question is put so briefly that a true answer counts against us, while a false one can be contradicted. In this dilemma, our safest, indeed our only, course seems to be to say something at all risks. Placed as we are, we could scarcely keep silent without being tormented by the damning thought that speaking might have saved us. Another difficulty we face is the difficulty of convincing you. If we were strangers to one another, we might benefit by bringing forward new matter you were unfamiliar with; as it is, we can tell you nothing you do not know already. Our fear is not that you have judged us, in your own minds, to have failed in our duty toward you and made this our crime, but that to please a third party we are being put through a trial whose result is already decided. Even so, we will set out before you what we can justly urge — not only on the question of the Thebans' quarrel with us, but addressing you and the rest of the Hellenes — and we will remind you of our good services and try to win you over.

“To your short question, whether we have done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in this war, we answer: if you ask us as enemies, then to refrain from serving you was not to do you injury; if as friends, then you are more in fault for marching against us. During the peace, and against the Mede, we acted well: we have not now been the first to break the peace, and we were the only Boeotians who then joined in defending the liberty of Hellas against the Mede. Although an inland people, we were present at the action at Artemisium; in the battle fought in our territory we fought beside you and Pausanias; and in all the other Hellenic exploits of the time, we took a part quite out of proportion to our strength. Besides, you, as Lacedaemonians, ought not to forget that at the time of the great panic at Sparta after the earthquake, caused by the secession of the Helots to Ithome, we sent a third of our citizens to assist you.

“On these great and historical occasions, such was the part we chose, even though we afterwards became your enemies. For this you were to blame. When we asked for your alliance against our Theban oppressors, you rejected our petition and told us to go to the Athenians, who were our neighbours, since you lived too far off. In the war we have never done you, and never would have done you, anything unreasonable. If we refused to desert the Athenians when you asked us to, we did no wrong; they had helped us against the Thebans when you drew back, and we could no longer give them up with honour, especially since we had obtained their alliance and been admitted to their citizenship at our own request, and after receiving benefits at their hands; it was plainly our duty to follow their orders loyally. Besides, the faults either of you may commit in your supremacy must be laid not on the followers but on the chiefs who lead them astray.

“As for the Thebans, they have wronged us again and again, and their last aggression — which is what has brought us into our present position — is within your own knowledge. By seizing our city in time of peace, and what is more at a holy time in the month, they justly met our vengeance, in accordance with the universal law that sanctions resistance to an invader. It cannot now be right that we should suffer on their account. By taking your own immediate interest and their animosity as the test of justice, you will prove yourselves rather servants of expediency than judges of right; even though they may seem useful to you now, we and the rest of the Hellenes gave you much more valuable help at a time of greater need. Now you are the aggressors, and others fear you; but at the crisis we are speaking of, when the barbarian threatened all with slavery, the Thebans were on his side. It is fair, therefore, to weigh our patriotism then against our error now, if error there has been. You will find the merit outweighing the fault, and displayed at a juncture when there were few Hellenes willing to set their valour against the strength of Xerxes, and when greater praise belonged to those who chose the dangerous path of honour over the safe course of consulting their own interest in the matter of the invasion. We were among those few, and we were highly honoured for it; and now we fear to perish by having again acted on the same principles and chosen to act well with Athens rather than wisely with Sparta. Yet in justice the same cases should be decided in the same way, and policy should mean nothing else than lasting gratitude for the service of a good ally combined with proper attention to one's own immediate interest.

“Consider too that at present the Hellenes generally regard you as a pattern of worth and honour; and if you pass an unjust sentence in this case — which is no obscure cause, but one in which you, the judges, are as illustrious as we, the prisoners, are blameless — beware that displeasure be not felt at an unworthy decision in the matter of honourable men, made by men yet more honourable than they, and at the consecration in the national temples of spoils taken from the Plataeans, the benefactors of Hellas. It will seem shocking indeed for Lacedaemonians to destroy Plataea, and for the city whose name your fathers inscribed upon the tripod at Delphi for its good service to be wiped by you off the map of Hellas, to please the Thebans. We have fallen so far that, while the success of the Medes was our ruin, the Thebans now supplant us in your once fond regard; and we have been subjected to two of the greatest dangers — that of dying of starvation then, if we had not surrendered our town, and now of being tried for our lives. So that we Plataeans, after exertions beyond our power in the cause of the Hellenes, are rejected by all, forsaken and unaided; helped by none of our allies, and reduced to doubting the firmness of our only hope, yourselves.

“Still, in the name of the gods who once presided over our confederacy, and of our own good service in the Hellenic cause, we beg you to relent: to reverse the decision we fear the Thebans may have obtained from you; to take back the gift you have given them, lest they disgrace you by killing us; to win a clean rather than a guilty gratitude, and not to gratify others only to be yourselves rewarded with shame. Our lives may be taken quickly, but it will be a heavy task to wipe away the infamy of the deed. We are no enemies whom you might justly punish, but friends forced to take up arms against you. To spare our lives would therefore be a just judgment, if you also consider that we are prisoners who surrendered of our own accord, stretching out our hands for quarter — whose slaughter Hellenic law forbids — and who besides were always your benefactors. Look at the sepulchres of your fathers, slain by the Medes and buried in our country, whom year by year we honoured with garments and all the other dues, and the first-fruits of all that our land produced in their season, as friends from a friendly country and allies to our old companions in arms. If you do not decide rightly, your conduct will be the very opposite of ours. Consider this: Pausanias buried them thinking he was laying them in friendly ground among friendly men; but if you kill us and turn Plataean territory into Theban land, you will be leaving your fathers and kinsmen in hostile soil and among their murderers, stripped of the honours they now enjoy. What is more, you will enslave the land in which the freedom of the Hellenes was won, leave desolate the temples of the gods to whom they prayed before defeating the Medes, and take away your ancestral sacrifices from the men who founded and instituted them.

“It would be no glory of yours, Lacedaemonians, either to offend in this way against the common law of the Hellenes and against your own ancestors, or to kill us, your benefactors, to gratify another's hatred when you have not been wronged yourselves. The greater glory would be to spare us and to yield to the impulse of reasonable compassion — reflecting not only on the awful fate that awaits us, but also on the character of the sufferers, and on the impossibility of predicting how soon misfortune may fall even on those who do not deserve it. We, as we have a right to do and as our need impels us, entreat you, calling aloud upon the gods at whose common altar all the Hellenes worship — to hear our request, to be not unmindful of the oaths your fathers swore, which we now plead. We supplicate you by the tombs of your fathers, and appeal to the dead to save us from falling into the hands of the Thebans, and from being given up — their dearest friends — to their most detested foes. We remind you too of that day on which we did the most glorious deeds at your fathers' sides, we who on this day are likely to suffer the most dreadful fate. Finally, to do what is necessary and yet most difficult for men in our situation — to make an end of speaking, since with that ending the danger to our lives draws near — we say in conclusion that we did not surrender our city to the Thebans (we would have preferred inglorious starvation to that), but trusted in you and capitulated to you. It would be just, if we fail to persuade you, to put us back in the same position and let us take whatever chance falls to us. And at the same time we beg you not to give us up — your suppliants, Lacedaemonians, out of your hands and out of your faith — Plataeans, foremost of the Hellenic patriots, to the Thebans, our most hated enemies. Be our saviours, and do not, while you free the rest of the Hellenes, bring us to destruction.”

Such were the words of the Plataeans. The Thebans, afraid that the Lacedaemonians might be moved by what they had heard, came forward and said that they too wished to address the assembly, since the Plataeans had, against their wishes, been allowed to speak at length instead of being held to a simple answer to the question. Leave being granted, the Thebans spoke as follows:

“We should never have asked to make this speech if the Plataeans on their side had been content with briefly answering the question, and had not turned around and made charges against us, coupled with a long defence of themselves on matters outside the present inquiry — matters not even the subject of accusation — and with praise of what no one finds fault with. However, since they have done so, we must answer their charges and refute their self-praise, so that neither our bad name nor their good repute may help them, but that you may hear the real truth on both points and so decide.

“The origin of our quarrel was this. We settled Plataea some time after the rest of Boeotia, together with other places out of which we had driven the mixed population. The Plataeans refused to recognize our supremacy, as had originally been arranged, and separated themselves from the rest of the Boeotians, proving traitors to their nationality. We used compulsion, on which they went over to the Athenians and with them did us much harm — for which we retaliated.

“Next, when the barbarian invaded Hellas, they say that they were the only Boeotians who did not Medize. This is where they most glorify themselves and most abuse us. Our reply is that if they did not Medize, it was because the Athenians did not do so either; just as afterwards, when the Athenians attacked the Hellenes, they, the Plataeans, were again the only Boeotians who Atticized. And yet consider the forms of our respective governments at the time we acted as we did. Our city at that juncture had neither an oligarchical constitution in which all the nobles enjoyed equal rights, nor a democracy, but that which is most opposed to law and good government, and nearest to a tyranny — the rule of a close cabal. These men, hoping to strengthen their personal power by the success of the Mede, kept down the people by force and brought him into the town. The city as a whole was not its own mistress when it acted in this way, and ought not to be reproached for the errors it committed while deprived of its constitution. Look only at how we acted after the departure of the Mede and the recovery of the constitution: when the Athenians attacked the rest of Hellas and tried to subjugate our country — most of which faction had already made them masters of — did we not fight and conquer at Coronea and free Boeotia? And do we not now actively contribute to the liberation of the rest, providing horses to the cause and a force unequalled by that of any other state in the confederacy?

“Let this suffice to excuse us for our Medism. We will now try to show that you have injured the Hellenes more than we have, and that you deserve condign punishment more than we do. It was in defence against us, you say, that you became allies and citizens of Athens. If so, you ought only to have called in the Athenians against us, instead of joining them in attacking others. You were free to do this if you ever felt that they were leading you where you did not wish to follow, since Lacedaemon was already your ally against the Mede, as you so much insist. That was surely enough to keep us off, and above all to allow you to deliberate in safety. Nevertheless, of your own choice and without compulsion, you chose to throw in your lot with Athens. You say it would have been base for you to betray your benefactors; but it was surely far baser and more iniquitous to sacrifice the whole body of the Hellenes, your fellow confederates who were liberating Hellas, than to sacrifice the Athenians alone, who were enslaving it. The return you made them was therefore neither equal nor honourable, since you called them in, as you say, because you were yourselves being oppressed, and then became their accomplices in oppressing others — though baseness consists rather in failing to return like for like than in failing to return what is justly due but would have to be unjustly paid.

“Meanwhile, after we have plainly shown that it was not for the sake of the Hellenes that you alone refused to Medize, but because the Athenians did not Medize either, and you wished to side with them and against the rest, you now claim the benefit of good deeds done to please your neighbours. This cannot be allowed. You chose the Athenians, and with them you must stand or fall. You cannot plead the league then made and claim that it should now protect you. You abandoned that league and offended against it by helping rather than hindering the subjugation of the Aeginetans and others of its members — and that not under compulsion, but while enjoying the same institutions you enjoy to the present hour, and with no one forcing you as we were forced. Lastly, an invitation was addressed to you, before you were blockaded, to be neutral and join neither party — and you did not accept it. Who then deserves the detestation of the Hellenes more than you, who sought their ruin under the mask of honour? The earlier virtues you claim you now show not to be proper to your character; the real bent of your nature has at last been damningly proved. When the Athenians took the path of injustice, you followed them.

“So much for our unwilling Medism and your wilful Atticizing. The last wrong you complain of consists in our having, as you say, lawlessly invaded your town in time of peace and festival. Here again we cannot think that we were more in fault than you yourselves. If on our own initiative we had made an armed attack on your city and ravaged your territory, we would be guilty. But if the first men among you in property and family — wishing to put an end to the foreign connection and to restore you to the common Boeotian country — of their own free will invited us in, where is our crime? Where wrong is done, those who lead, as you say, are more to blame than those who follow. Not that, in our judgment, any wrong was done either by them or by us. Citizens like yourselves, and with more at stake than you, they opened their own walls and brought us into their own city — not as enemies but as friends — to prevent the bad among you from becoming worse, to give honest men their due, to reform principles without attacking persons; for you were not to be banished from your city, but brought home to your kindred, nor made enemies to any, but friends alike to all.

“That our intention was not hostile is proved by our conduct. We did no harm to anyone, but publicly invited those who wished to live under a national, Boeotian government to come over to us. At first you gladly did so, made an agreement with us, and stayed quiet — until you saw how few of us there were. Now there may possibly have been something not quite fair in our entering without the consent of your commons. But you did not repay us in kind. Instead of refraining, as we had done, from violence, and persuading us to withdraw by negotiation, you fell on us in breach of your agreement, and killed some of us in the fight — of which we do not greatly complain, for in that there was a certain justice. But others who held out their hands and were given quarter, and whose lives you subsequently promised us, you lawlessly butchered. If this was not abominable, what is? And after these three crimes committed one after the other — the breach of your agreement, the murder of the men afterwards, and the lying breach of your promise not to kill them if we refrained from damaging your property in the country — you still maintain that we are the criminals, and pretend that you yourselves should escape justice. Not so, if these your judges decide rightly; you will be punished for them all together.

“Such, Lacedaemonians, are the facts. We have gone into them at some length both on your account and on our own, so that you may feel that you will justly condemn the prisoners, and we, that we have given an additional sanction to our vengeance. We would also keep you from being moved by hearing of their past virtues, if any such they had: these may fairly be appealed to by the victims of injustice, but they only aggravate the guilt of criminals, since the criminals offend against their own better nature. Nor let them gain anything by crying and wailing, by calling on your fathers' tombs and on their own desolate condition. Against this we point to the far more dreadful fate of our young men, butchered at their hands; the fathers of these — some of whom fell at Coronea, bringing Boeotia over to you, while others sit forlorn old men by desolate hearths — have far more reason to implore your justice on the prisoners. The pity that the Plataeans appeal to is rather due to those who suffer unworthily; those who suffer justly, as these men do, are on the contrary subjects for triumph. Their present desolate condition is their own doing, since they wilfully rejected the better alliance. Their lawless act was not provoked by any action of ours; hatred, not justice, inspired their decision; and even now the satisfaction they afford us is not adequate. They will suffer by a legal sentence — not, as they pretend, as suppliants asking for quarter in battle, but as prisoners who surrendered on agreement to take their trial. Vindicate, then, Lacedaemonians, the Hellenic law they have broken, and grant to us, the victims of its violation, the reward our zeal deserves. Do not let us be supplanted in your favour by their harangues; offer instead an example to the Hellenes, that the contests to which you invite them are contests of deeds, not words. Good deeds can be briefly stated, but where wrong is done, a wealth of language is needed to veil its deformity. If, however, leading powers were to do what you are now doing — putting one short question to all alike and deciding accordingly — men would be less tempted to seek fine phrases to cover bad actions.”

Such were the words of the Thebans. The Lacedaemonian judges decided that the question whether they had received any service from the Plataeans in the war was a fair one to put, since they had always invited the Plataeans to be neutral, in keeping with the original covenant of Pausanias after the defeat of the Mede, and had again definitely offered them the same conditions before the blockade. That offer having been refused, they were now, they considered, by the loyalty of their intention, released from the covenant; and having, as they considered, suffered evil at the Plataeans' hands, they brought them in again one by one and asked each the same question — whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in the war — and on their saying that they had not, took them out and killed them, all without exception. The number of Plataeans massacred this way was not less than two hundred, with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The city the Thebans gave for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit, and afterwards razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Onto the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches which they dedicated to Hera, for whom they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten-year lease to Theban occupiers. The adverse attitude of the Lacedaemonians in the whole Plataean affair was mainly adopted to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.

Meanwhile, the forty Peloponnesian ships that had gone to the relief of the Lesbians — and which we left flying across the open sea, pursued by the Athenians — were caught in a storm off Crete, and scattering from there, made their way to the Peloponnese, where they found at Cyllene thirteen Leucadian and Ambraciot galleys, with Brasidas, son of Tellis, lately arrived as counsellor to Alcidas. The Lacedaemonians, on the failure of the Lesbian expedition, had resolved to strengthen their fleet and sail to Corcyra, where a revolution had broken out, in order to arrive there before the twelve Athenian ships at Naupactus could be reinforced from Athens. Brasidas and Alcidas accordingly began their preparations.

The Corcyraean revolution began with the return of the prisoners taken in the sea-fights off Epidamnus. The Corinthians had released these men, nominally on the security of eight hundred talents put up by their proxeni, but in reality on their undertaking to bring Corcyra over to Corinth. These men set to work canvassing each of the citizens and intriguing to detach the city from Athens. On the arrival of an Athenian and a Corinthian vessel, with envoys on board, a conference was held in which the Corcyraeans voted to remain allies of the Athenians according to their agreement, but to be friends of the Peloponnesians, as they had been before. Meanwhile, the returned prisoners brought Peithias, a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and leader of the commons, to trial on the charge of enslaving Corcyra to Athens. Acquitted, he retorted by charging five of the wealthiest of their number with cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous, the legal penalty being a stater for each stake. They were convicted, and the amount of the penalty being very large, they seated themselves as suppliants in the temples to be allowed to pay it by instalments. But Peithias, who was one of the senate, persuaded that body to enforce the law; on which the accused, made desperate by the law, and also learning that Peithias intended, while still a member of the senate, to persuade the people to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with Athens, banded together, armed with daggers, and suddenly bursting into the senate, killed Peithias and sixty others — senators and private citizens. Only a few of Peithias's party took refuge in the Athenian galley, which had not yet sailed.

After this outrage, the conspirators summoned the Corcyraeans to an assembly and said that what they had done would turn out for the best, and would save them from being enslaved by Athens. For the future, they moved that neither party should be received unless they came peacefully in a single ship, any larger number being treated as enemies. They made this motion and forced it through, and at once sent off envoys to Athens to justify what had been done and to dissuade the refugees there from any hostile proceedings that might lead to a reaction.

On the arrival of the embassy, the Athenians arrested the envoys and all who listened to them as revolutionists, and lodged them in Aegina. Meanwhile, a Corinthian galley arrived in the island with Lacedaemonian envoys, and the dominant Corcyraean party attacked the commons and defeated them in battle. Night coming on, the commons took refuge in the Acropolis and the higher parts of the city, and concentrated themselves there, also holding the Hyllaic harbour. Their adversaries occupied the marketplace, where most of them lived, and the harbour next to it, facing the mainland.

The next day passed in skirmishes of little importance, each party sending out into the country to offer freedom to the slaves and to invite them to join them. The mass of the slaves answered the appeal of the commons; their opponents were reinforced by eight hundred mercenaries from the mainland.

After a day's interval, hostilities resumed, with victory remaining with the commons, who had the advantage in numbers and position, the women also valiantly assisting them by pelting tiles from the houses and supporting the melee with a fortitude beyond their sex. Toward dusk, the oligarchs, in full rout and fearing that the victorious commons might assault and take the arsenal and put them to the sword, set fire to the houses around the marketplace and the lodging-houses to bar their advance, sparing neither their own nor those of their neighbours. Much of the merchants' stock was consumed, and the city would have risked total destruction had a wind come up to help the flame by blowing on it. Hostilities now ceased; both sides kept quiet, passing the night on guard, while the Corinthian ship slipped out to sea on the victory of the commons, and most of the mercenaries crossed secretly over to the mainland.

The next day the Athenian general Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian heavy infantry. He at once tried to bring about a settlement and persuaded the two parties to agree to bring to trial ten of the ringleaders — who promptly fled — while the rest were to live in peace, coming to terms with each other and entering into a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians. This arranged, he was about to sail away when the leaders of the commons induced him to leave them five of his ships, so as to make their adversaries less inclined to make a move, while they would man and send with him an equal number of their own. He had no sooner consented than they began enrolling their enemies for the ships; and these, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of the Dioscuri. An attempt by Nicostratus to reassure them and persuade them to rise proved unsuccessful, and the commons, taking this as a pretext, armed themselves, alleging the refusal of their adversaries to sail with them as proof of the hollowness of their intentions. They took their arms out of their houses and would have killed some whom they fell in with, if Nicostratus had not prevented it. The rest of the party, seeing what was going on, seated themselves as suppliants in the temple of Hera, no fewer than four hundred in number; until the commons, fearing they might adopt some desperate resolution, induced them to rise and conveyed them over to the island in front of the temple, where provisions were sent across to them.

At this stage in the revolution, on the fourth or fifth day after the removal of the men to the island, the Peloponnesian ships arrived from Cyllene, where they had been stationed since their return from Ionia. There were fifty-three of them, still under the command of Alcidas, but with Brasidas also on board as his adviser. Dropping anchor at Sybota, a harbour on the mainland, at daybreak they made sail for Corcyra.

The Corcyraeans, in great confusion and alarm at the state of things in the city and at the approach of the invader, at once set about equipping sixty vessels, which they sent out, as fast as they were manned, against the enemy, despite the Athenians recommending that they let them sail out first and follow themselves afterwards with all their ships together. As their vessels came up to the enemy in this straggling fashion, two immediately deserted; in others the crews were fighting among themselves, and there was no order in anything that was done. So the Peloponnesians, seeing their confusion, placed twenty ships to oppose the Corcyraeans, and ranged the rest against the twelve Athenian ships, among which were the two vessels Salaminia and Paralus.

While the Corcyraeans, attacking without judgment and in small detachments, were already crippled by their own misconduct, the Athenians, afraid of the numbers of the enemy and of being surrounded, did not venture to attack the main body or even the centre of the division opposed to them. Instead they fell on its wing and sank one vessel; after which the Peloponnesians formed in a circle, and the Athenians rowed round them and tried to throw them into disorder. Seeing this, the division opposed to the Corcyraeans, fearing a repeat of the disaster of Naupactus, came up to support their friends, and the whole fleet now bore down united on the Athenians, who retired before it, backing water and withdrawing as leisurely as possible to give the Corcyraeans time to escape, while the enemy was kept occupied. Such was the character of this sea-fight, which lasted until sunset.

The Corcyraeans now feared that the enemy would follow up their victory and sail against the town and rescue the men in the island, or strike some other equally decisive blow; so they carried the men over again to the temple of Hera, and kept guard over the city. The Peloponnesians, however, although victorious in the sea-fight, did not venture to attack the town, but took the thirteen Corcyraean vessels they had captured and sailed back with them to the mainland from which they had set out. The next day they likewise refrained from attacking the city, although the disorder and panic were at their height, and although Brasidas, it is said, urged Alcidas, his superior officer, to attack; instead they landed at the promontory of Leukimme and laid waste the country.

Meanwhile the commons in Corcyra, still in great fear of the fleet attacking them, came to a parley with the suppliants and their friends in order to save the town, and persuaded some of them to go on board the ships, of which they still manned thirty, against the expected attack. But the Peloponnesians, after ravaging the country until midday, sailed away, and toward nightfall were informed by beacon signals of the approach of sixty Athenian vessels from Leucas, under the command of Eurymedon, son of Thucles, which had been sent off by the Athenians on news of the revolution and of the fleet under Alcidas being about to sail for Corcyra.

The Peloponnesians accordingly set off in haste at once for home by night, coasting along the shore, and to avoid being seen rounding the Isthmus of Leucas, they hauled their ships across it and so departed. The Corcyraeans, made aware of the approach of the Athenian fleet and the departure of the enemy, brought the Messenians from outside the walls into the town, and ordered the fleet they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbour. While it was doing so, they killed any of their enemies they could lay hands on, dispatching afterwards, as they landed them, those whom they had persuaded to go on board the ships. Next they went to the sanctuary of Hera and persuaded about fifty men to take their trial, and condemned them all to death. The mass of the suppliants who refused to do this, on seeing what was happening, killed each other there in the consecrated ground; some hanged themselves on the trees, and others destroyed themselves in whatever way they could. During the seven days that Eurymedon stayed with his sixty ships, the Corcyraeans were busy butchering those of their fellow citizens whom they regarded as their enemies. Although the crime alleged was an attempt to overturn the democracy, some were also killed for private hatred, others by their debtors because of the money owed to them. Death thus raged in every shape; and, as usually happens at such times, there was no length to which violence did not go: sons were killed by their fathers, suppliants were dragged from the altar or slain on it, and some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there.

So bloody was the course of the revolution, and the impression it made was the greater because it was one of the first to occur. Later, one may say, the whole Hellenic world was convulsed; struggles being everywhere made by the popular leaders to bring in the Athenians, and by the oligarchs to bring in the Lacedaemonians. In peace there would have been neither the pretext nor the wish to make such an invitation; but in war, with an alliance always at the disposal of either faction for the harm of their adversaries and their own corresponding advantage, opportunities for bringing in the foreigner were never wanting to the revolutionary parties. The sufferings that revolution brought on the cities were many and terrible, such as have occurred and always will occur as long as the nature of mankind remains the same — though in a more severe or milder form, varying in their symptoms with the variety of cases. In peace and prosperity, states and individuals have better sentiments, because they are not suddenly confronted with imperious necessities; but war takes away the easy supply of daily wants, and so proves a rough master that brings most men's characters down to the level of their fortunes. Revolution thus ran its course from city to city, and the places it reached last, having heard what had been done before, carried the refinement of their inventions to still greater excess, as shown in the cunning of their enterprises and the atrocity of their reprisals. Words had to change their ordinary meaning and to take that which was now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation, a cloak for unmanliness; ability to see all sides of a question, an inability to act on any. Frantic violence became the attribute of manliness; cautious plotting, a justifiable means of self-defence. The advocate of extreme measures was always trustworthy; his opponent a man to be suspected. To succeed in a plot was to have a shrewd head; to detect one, a still shrewder. But to try to provide against having to do either was to break up your party and to fear your adversaries. In short, to forestall an intending criminal, or to suggest the idea of a crime where it was not yet there, was equally commended — until even blood became a weaker tie than party, from the superior readiness of those united by the latter to dare anything without reserve. Such associations had not in view the blessings derived from established institutions, but were formed by ambition for their overthrow; and the confidence of their members in each other rested less on any religious sanction than on shared complicity in crime. The fair proposals of an adversary were met by the stronger of the two with jealous precautions, not with a generous confidence. Revenge also was held of more account than self-preservation. Oaths of reconciliation, offered on either side only to meet an immediate difficulty, held good only as long as no other weapon was at hand; but when opportunity offered, he who first ventured to seize it and catch his enemy off guard thought this perfidious vengeance sweeter than an open one, since, considerations of safety apart, success by treachery won him the palm of superior intelligence. Indeed it is generally the case that men are readier to call rogues clever than simpletons honest, and are as ashamed of being the second as they are proud of being the first. The cause of all these evils was the lust for power arising from greed and ambition; and from these passions proceeded the violence of parties once engaged in contention. The leaders in the cities, each side equipped with the fairest professions — on the one side the cry of political equality of the people, on the other a moderate aristocracy — sought prizes for themselves in those public interests they pretended to cherish, and, recoiling from no means in their struggles for ascendancy, engaged in the direst excesses. In their acts of vengeance they went to even greater lengths, not stopping at what justice or the good of the state demanded, but making the party caprice of the moment their only standard, and invoking with equal readiness the condemnation of an unjust verdict or the authority of the strong arm to glut the animosities of the hour. So religion was in honour with neither party, but the use of fair phrases to arrive at guilty ends was in high reputation. Meanwhile the moderate part of the citizens perished between the two, either for not joining in the quarrel, or because envy would not suffer them to escape.

Thus every form of iniquity took root in the Hellenic countries because of the troubles. The ancient simplicity into which honour so largely entered was laughed out and vanished; and society became divided into camps in which no man trusted his fellow. To put an end to this, there was no promise that could be depended on, nor oath that could command respect; but all parties, dwelling rather on the hopelessness of a permanent state of things in their calculations, were more intent on self-defence than capable of confidence. In this contest, the blunter wits were most successful. Apprehensive of their own deficiencies and of the cleverness of their antagonists, they feared to be worsted in debate and surprised by the combinations of their more versatile opponents, and so at once boldly had recourse to action; while their adversaries, arrogantly assuming that they would know in time and that it was unnecessary to secure by action what policy afforded, often fell victims to their lack of precaution.

Meanwhile Corcyra gave the first example of most of the crimes referred to: the reprisals exacted by the governed who had never experienced equitable treatment or indeed anything but insolence from their rulers — when their hour came; the iniquitous resolves of those who desired to be rid of their accustomed poverty, and ardently coveted their neighbours' goods; and lastly, the savage and pitiless excesses into which men who had begun the struggle, not in a class but in a party spirit, were hurried by their ungovernable passions. In the confusion into which life was now thrown in the cities, human nature, always in revolt against the law and now its master, gladly showed itself ungoverned in passion, above respect for justice, and the enemy of all superiority; for revenge would not have been set above religion, nor gain above justice, had it not been for the fatal power of envy. Indeed, men too often take it upon themselves, in the prosecution of their revenge, to set the example of doing away with those general laws to which all alike can look for salvation in adversity, instead of allowing them to subsist against the day of danger when their aid may be required.

While the revolutionary passions were thus displaying themselves for the first time in the factions of Corcyra, Eurymedon and the Athenian fleet sailed away. After this, some five hundred Corcyraean exiles who had succeeded in escaping took some forts on the mainland, and, becoming masters of the Corcyraean territory across the water, made this their base for plundering their countrymen on the island, and did so much damage as to cause a severe famine in the town. They also sent envoys to Lacedaemon and Corinth to negotiate their restoration, but meeting with no success, afterwards collected boats and mercenaries and crossed over to the island, about six hundred in all. They burned their boats, so as to have no hope except in becoming masters of the country, went up to Mount Istone, and fortifying themselves there began to harass those in the city and gained command of the country.

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships under the command of Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus, to Sicily, where the Syracusans and Leontines were at war. The Syracusans had for allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina — these had been included in the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had not taken any active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians were for the Syracusans, the Rhegians for their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens and appealed to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin to persuade the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality to prevent the exportation of Sicilian corn to the Peloponnese and to test the possibility of bringing Sicily into subjection. Accordingly they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.
